gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Schumacher's plug-in 'engine start' amps are not the same kind of rating as a lithium pack's 'peak amps'. The SC1281/SC1309 rate is a capped current fed from the wall. It flows for up to 7 seconds per crank, and if the starter draws more than that rate the crank can last less than 3 seconds. Repeated cranks then trigger a 3-minute cool-down. A pack's '1,000 A peak' is a brief maximum, so 100 A vs 1,000 A is not a 10× difference in starting power.
standout_why: Cited rivals: the schumacherelectric.com Battery Chargers archive returned HTTP 429 when opened today, so it is unverified. The Advance Auto SC1309 page timed out, also unverified; the only things known about it are its title and ChatGPT's summary, which give 6/2/40/200A ratings and no cranking time. Top results opened: Clamp & Crank (2026-09-29) puts SC1281 '100 A' engine start next to GB40 '1,000 A' peak without saying whether the two are comparable. BatteryTrail (2026-10-28) gives only a generic 3 to 5 second crank limit, and AutoGearLab (2026-09-04) says only that chargers 'commonly specify limits'. PlainPrepper has the SC1281's 7-second crank and 3-minute cool-down. None of them explains that a crank draw above the engine-start rate shortens the crank to under 3 seconds, or that engine-start amps and peak amps are different kinds of rating.
decides: This confirms that the plug-in Schumacher combos (SC1281 at 100 A, SC1309 at 200 A) suit a shopper who has an outlet and time. The charger gives a capped, timed boost with a 2-minute wait before cranking, and on a hard-to-turn engine the crank can drop below 3 seconds. A shopper who needs a strong start away from an outlet should not choose by comparing the 100 A or 200 A figure with a pack's peak amps. They should choose a lithium pack or a pack-plus-charger unit such as the Battery Tender CNS 4120. The page should footnote the amp column as 'charger engine-start rate (AC, capped, 7-second crank) vs pack peak (instantaneous)'.

findings.label: Engine-start crank limit per attempt
findings.value: 7 s (crank 'until it starts or 7 seconds pass')
findings.source_title: Schumacher Electric SC1281 Owner's Manual, page 9 (ManualsLib)

findings.label: Cool-down after repeated cranking
findings.value: 180 s mandatory cool-down after repeated cranking within a 3-minute ready period
findings.source_title: Schumacher Electric SC1281 Owner's Manual, page 9 (ManualsLib)
findings.note: The manual says not to crank during the cool-down. For a battery under 2 V or in extreme cold, it says to charge for 5 minutes before cranking.

findings.label: Crank time when the starter draws more than the engine-start rate
findings.source_title: Schumacher Electric SC1281 Owner's Manual, page 12, troubleshooting (ManualsLib)
findings.note: Manual wording: 'If cranking draws more than the Engine Start Rate, crank time may be less than 3 seconds.' This shows the 100 A figure is a capped supply rate with a time limit, not a surge rating like a pack's peak amps.

findings.label: Engine-start sequence
findings.value: 2 min of charging before 'rdy', then up to 7 s of cranking at 'up to its maximum output', then a 180 s cool-down after repeated cranks; needs a grounded 120 V outlet
findings.source_title: Schumacher Electric SC1309 Owner's Manual, page 10 of 30 (ManualsLib)
findings.note: Same timed logic as the SC1281. The SC1309's 200 A rating (from ChatGPT's answer and the Advance Auto title) is delivered only while the unit is plugged in.

findings.label: Rated engine-start current as a reviewer lists it, next to pack peak ratings
findings.value: 100 A engine start vs NOCO GB40 1,000 A peak, DEWALT DXAEJ14 1,600 A peak, STANLEY J7CS 700 A peak / 350 A instant
findings.source_title: Best Jump Starter and Battery Charger Combos | Clamp & Crank
findings.note: Clamp & Crank lists these figures side by side without saying whether they measure the same thing. STANLEY's own '700 peak / 350 instant' split shows that peak can be about twice the usable starting figure for the same pack.

findings.label: AC input draw
findings.value: 4 A continuous, 20 A intermittent at 120 V AC
findings.source_title: Battery Charger and Jump Starter: Plug-In vs Built-In Pack | PlainPrepper
findings.note: Named reviewer page. 20 A × 120 V = 2,400 W of wall input during engine start, so a weak extension cord or a shared garage circuit can limit it. The figure was not checked against Schumacher's spec table, which returned HTTP 429.

findings.label: Combined ratings and crank guidance
findings.value: 4 A charger plus 1,200 A internal lithium jump pack; crank up to 5 s with 30 s between attempts
findings.source_title: Battery Charger and Jump Starter: Plug-In vs Built-In Pack | PlainPrepper
findings.note: Pack-based: it jumps from its own battery rather than from the wall, so it has a shorter rest (30 s vs 180 s) but a peak-type amp rating. The maker's page returned HTTP 429.
